# Agent Harness Guardrails and Hooks

Rules for harnesses that run autonomous Claude Code agents. Each rule:
pattern, why, when to apply.

> Learned while building an autonomous agent harness on Windows 11.

## Enforce With Hooks, Not Instructions

**Pattern:** any behavior that must always hold is a hook. Guard hooks (deny
rules) **fail closed**: unparsable input or an internal error denies. State and
notification hooks **fail open**: they never block work.

**Why:** a reminder in a prompt gets forgotten under context pressure. A hook
does not.

**When:** security boundaries, model/tool restrictions, protected paths.

## Absolute Interpreter Paths in Hook Commands

**Pattern:** reference the interpreter by absolute path (for example the full
path to `node`), not by bare name.

**Why:** on a stale or minimal `PATH` the interpreter is missing, the hook
errors as a non-blocking failure, and the guard silently fails open.

**When:** every hook `command`.

## Test Guards in the Real Layout

**Pattern:** besides unit tests with simulated input, run each guard against
the real agent working directory and file layout.

**Why:** a shell-write guard passed unit tests but was allowed live: the
agent's working directory was the parent of the repo and the guard searched
only upward from it.

**When:** any guard that resolves paths relative to the working directory.

## Isolate Live State in Hook Tests

**Pattern:** tests save, clear, and restore every live state file the hooks
read or write. Give shared files an environment-variable seam so tests point
at a temp copy.

**Why:** a live process rewrote the same file mid-test, and real state leaked
into assertions.

**When:** any test that runs hooks on a machine where the harness is also live.

## Hash Locked Test Files With Normalized Line Endings

**Pattern:** hash text files after normalizing CRLF to LF. Hash binaries by
exact bytes.

**Why:** `git checkout` with `autocrlf` rewrites line endings, and a byte hash
then reports a false change to a locked file.

**When:** any check that detects edits to protected test files.

## Never Certify Your Own Work

**Pattern:** an independent evaluator (fresh context, skeptical prompt) reviews
each build. It sees the spec and the code, not the builder's claims. Every
defect it finds gets a failing-first regression test before the fix.

**Why:** in one project the evaluator found 8 defects, two high severity, in
code the builder had reported green.

**When:** every non-trivial build, before it is called done.

## A Passing Doc Claim Is Not Evidence

**Pattern:** verify tool flags and behavior with a real run, not the docs
alone.

**Why:** one real run exposed a missing fallback that every unit test missed.

**When:** before relying on a flag, API, or documented behavior in a harness.
